title: Re-planning after a review
blurb: Explain why activities may be re-planned after a review, and how re-planning restores a realistic baseline under control.
question: At a gate review for a new visitor centre, the board approves continuation but cuts the remaining budget by 10% and asks for the centre to open before the summer season. Why may activities be re-planned after a review, and how should it be done?

teach.body: Re-planning means revising the plan (activities, sequence, resources, dates and budget) when a review shows the current plan is no longer realistic, or no longer the best way to meet the objectives. Typical triggers: variances, changes in scope or the business case, new risks or issues, resource changes, lessons from the review, a changed external environment, or a decision at a gate. In plain English: change the route when the road changes. Done through change control, it restores a realistic baseline.

children.sub: Scope or business case change; gate decision

children.label: Uncertainty

teach.h: From review finding to re-planning response
head: Review finding
Likely re-planning
rows: Reduce or re-phase scope, or stop
Add activities; update risk and quality

teach.h: Re-planning is healthy, if it is controlled
teach.body: Re-planning is not failure: reporting against a plan everyone knows is unrealistic is meaningless and hides the real position. But a new baseline must go through change control and be approved at the right level, with the business case re-checked and every affected part of the integrated plan updated. Keep the original baseline for comparison and lessons. Quietly resetting the baseline to make variances disappear ('moving the goalposts') undermines governance.

steps.label: Approve
steps.sub: at the right level of authority

steps.label: Communicate
steps.sub: everyone works to the new plan

teach.caption: After the gate, fit-out was fast-tracked to overlap the structure (adding risk) and the café moved to phase 2, so the centre opens in month 9 within the reduced budget.

teach.text: Three traps. Re-planning the schedule but leaving the business case and other plans untouched. Re-baselining informally so variances vanish. And assuming re-planning only follows bad news: a review may also reveal an opportunity, such as finishing early or adding value, that justifies re-planning.

teach.h: Re-planning in linear and iterative life cycles

rows.label: What changes
values: Backlog priorities for next time box

teach.body: At the gate before fit-out, the board approves continuation but cuts the remaining budget by 10% and wants opening before the summer season. The PM re-plans: the café fit-out moves to a second phase, exhibition fit-out is fast-tracked to overlap the structure, signage is re-procured, and the risk register adds the overlap risk. The sponsor confirms the business case still holds, approves the new baseline, and the revised plan goes to contractors and the tourism board.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the trigger, e.g. 'a gate decision cut the budget', then explain why the old plan no longer works.
Make each point a distinct reason: variance, scope or business case change, new risk, resources, lessons, external change.
State the purpose: restoring a realistic, achievable baseline that still meets the objectives.
Mention control: the new plan is approved through change control and communicated.
For iterative projects, note that re-planning is built in at every time box.
Re-plan when a review shows the plan is no longer realistic or no longer the best route to the objectives.
Triggers: variances, scope or business case changes, new risks or issues, resource changes, lessons, external change, gate decisions.
Re-planning restores a realistic baseline, approved through change control.
Update every affected part of the integrated plan, including the business case; keep the old baseline for comparison.
Iterative projects re-plan every time box by re-prioritising the backlog; time and cost stay fixed.

summary: You can now explain why activities may be re-planned after a review: variances, changes in scope or the business case, new risks or issues, resource changes, lessons learned, external change and gate decisions. You can also explain how re-planning should be controlled so it restores a realistic baseline rather than hiding problems.

A.q: Which is the BEST description of why activities may be re-planned after a review?
options: To make adverse variances disappear from reports
To restore a realistic, achievable plan
To move accountability to the review team
To avoid having to use change control
A.why: Re-planning restores a realistic baseline when the review shows the current plan no longer reflects reality or the best route to the objectives.

whyNot.0: Re-planning to hide variances misleads decision-makers and undermines governance.
whyNot.2: Accountability stays with the PM and sponsor; reviewers advise.
whyNot.3: Re-planning that changes the baseline goes through change control.

A.q: Which is NOT a typical reason for re-planning activities after a review?
options: A significant schedule variance
A change to the business case
New risks identified by the review
A wish for a greener RAG status
A.why: Re-planning responds to genuine changes in the project's situation, not to a wish for better-looking reports.

whyNot.0: Significant variances are a classic trigger for re-planning.
whyNot.1: If the business case changes, the plan must be revisited to stay aligned.
whyNot.2: New risks may need new activities, resources or contingency.

A.q: When activities are re-planned and a new baseline is needed, how should it be done?
options: Through change control, with approval
By the team, without telling the sponsor
By deleting the original baseline record
By the supplier, as they do the work
A.why: A new baseline is approved through change control at the right level of authority, then communicated to everyone affected.

whyNot.1: Changing the baseline without the sponsor bypasses governance.
whyNot.2: The original baseline is kept for comparison and lessons.
whyNot.3: Suppliers contribute, but the project's baseline is approved through its own governance.

B.q: A mid-project review finds that testing on the first software module took twice as long as estimated. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Assume the next modules will be quicker
Cut testing on the remaining modules
Re-estimate remaining testing and re-plan
Report the variance only at project closure
B.why: A lesson from the review is used to re-estimate the remaining work, so the plan becomes realistic again.

whyNot.0: Assuming improvement without evidence repeats the original estimating error.
whyNot.1: Cutting testing threatens quality and acceptance.
whyNot.3: Waiting until closure removes any chance to act on the variance.

B.q: At a gate review, the board approves continuation but halves the remaining contingency. What is the most likely consequence for the plan?
options: No change, as contingency is never used
Risk responses and the plan need revisiting
The project must now be stopped immediately
The team should work unpaid overtime
B.why: Less contingency means less cover for risks, so risk responses, scope or schedule may need re-planning to keep the project achievable.

whyNot.0: Contingency exists to be drawn down for risks; halving it matters.
whyNot.2: The board approved continuation, so stopping is not the consequence.
whyNot.3: Unpaid overtime is neither a planning response nor acceptable practice.

B.q: In an iterative project, a time-box review shows users now value a reporting feature more than planned. How is this usually re-planned?
options: The backlog is re-prioritised for next time
The fixed end date is moved back a month
A full re-baseline is approved by the board
The feature waits until the project closes
B.why: Iterative projects re-plan routinely: the product owner re-prioritises the backlog, and time and cost stay fixed.

whyNot.1: Time boxes and end dates are fixed in iterative working; scope flexes instead.
whyNot.2: Formal re-baselining is reserved for changes to fixed time, cost or objectives.
whyNot.3: Valuable features can be brought forward; delaying them loses early value.

C.q: A project manager quietly resets the schedule baseline each month so that no variance ever appears in reports. What is the main problem?
options: It makes the Gantt chart too hard to read
It breaches the supplier's contract terms
It means float is calculated incorrectly
It hides performance and bypasses control
C.why: Re-baselining without change control hides real performance from the sponsor and board and undermines governance.

whyNot.0: Readability is not the issue; the real problem is misleading decision-makers.
whyNot.1: Contracts may or may not be affected; the core problem is governance.
whyNot.2: Float may still be calculated correctly from the new dates; the issue is concealment.

C.q: A health check finds that a new building regulation will apply before handover. What is the most appropriate re-planning response?
options: Assess impact, then add work via change control
Ignore it, as it was not in the original scope
Ask the contractor to absorb it without cost
Delay the decision until the post-project review
C.why: An external change is a valid trigger: assess the impact on time, cost, quality and risk, then re-plan through change control.

whyNot.1: Compliance is not optional; the scope must change to meet the regulation.
whyNot.2: Who pays depends on the contract; it still needs assessing and re-planning.
whyNot.3: By then the project would have handed over non-compliant outputs.

C.q: Which THREE are valid reasons to re-plan activities after a review? (1) a change in the external environment (2) a key resource becoming unavailable (3) a decision taken at a gate (4) the sponsor preferring a greener report
options: 1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 3
2, 3 and 4
C.why: External change, resource changes and gate decisions are all genuine triggers. Wanting a greener report is not.

whyNot.0: Item 4 is wrong: re-planning should not be used to improve appearances.
whyNot.1: Item 4 is wrong, and item 2 (a resource becoming unavailable) is missing.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is wrong, and item 1 (external change) is missing.

reteach.title: Think of a music festival
reteach.question: Two weeks before a three-day festival, the organisers review their plan: the forecast is dire, the headliner has cancelled and ticket sales are 20% down. Why do they re-plan, and how?

blocks.body: Each finding breaks part of the plan. The forecast (external environment) means more trackway and covered stages. The cancelled headliner (resource change) means a new act and a revised running order. Lower sales (the business case) mean cutting the fourth stage to protect the budget. The organisers agree the changes, update the budget, site map and timetable together, and tell traders, crews and ticket holders. Carrying on with the old plan would be the real risk.

head: Review finding
Re-planning response
rows: Update budget, map, timetable; tell everyone

blocks.text: Rewriting only the timetable while the budget and site map still assume four stages is the festival version of re-planning the schedule but not the business case.

explain.body: When a review shows time, cost or quality has drifted from the baseline, the remaining work is re-planned: re-sequencing, fast-tracking (overlapping activities), crashing (adding resources at a cost) or re-estimating.

test.q: A review shows a critical-path activity is four weeks late. Which re-planning options are most relevant?
options: Close the project and restart it
Remove the activity from the plan
Re-sequence, fast-track or crash
Report it only if it gets worse
test.why: Schedule optimisation (re-sequencing, fast-tracking or crashing) can recover time on the critical path.

whyNot.0: Restarting wastes the work done and is not proportionate to a delay.
whyNot.1: Removing a needed activity leaves a gap in scope.
whyNot.3: A critical-path slip already affects the end date and needs action now.

explain.body: A gate decision, a scope change or a change to the business case can mean the old plan no longer serves the objectives. The business case is re-checked, scope and budget revised, and a new baseline approved.

test.q: Why must the business case be checked when a project is re-planned after a gate?
options: Because the PM owns the business case
Because suppliers must sign it off
Because it is rewritten each month
To confirm it is still justified
test.why: A re-plan changes costs, timings or benefits, so the sponsor must confirm the project is still worth doing.

whyNot.0: The sponsor owns the business case; the PM provides input.
whyNot.1: Suppliers do not sign off the client's business case.
whyNot.2: It is reviewed at gates and when significant changes occur, not monthly by default.

explain.h: Risks, resources, lessons and the environment
explain.body: New risks or issues, people or equipment becoming unavailable, lessons from the review, and changes outside the project (regulation, markets, weather) can all make the existing plan unrealistic.

test.q: A review's lessons show that suppliers on this project consistently deliver two weeks late. What is the best re-planning response?
options: Change suppliers on every remaining order
Build realistic lead times into the plan
Remove all supplier-dependent activities
Record it for the post-project review only
test.why: Using the lesson to set realistic lead times makes the remaining plan achievable.

whyNot.0: Switching every supplier mid-project may add more risk and delay than it removes.
whyNot.2: Supplier-dependent work is still needed to deliver the scope.
whyNot.3: Recording it without acting wastes the lesson for this project.

explain.body: A new baseline is approved through change control, every affected plan is updated, and the change is communicated. The original baseline is kept so performance and lessons can still be traced.

test.q: What should happen to the original baseline when a new one is approved?
options: It is deleted so that nobody gets confused
It is given to the supplier to keep
It replaces the new one at closure
It is kept for comparison and lessons
test.why: Keeping the original baseline preserves the audit trail and allows performance and lessons to be traced.

whyNot.0: Deleting it destroys the audit trail.
whyNot.1: Baseline records belong to the project, not the supplier.
whyNot.2: The approved new baseline is the one used going forward.
